note: Read for the paper's related work: each abstract page fetched directly on 2026-11-28 and hashed as fetched; every passage found again, whitespace aside, in the page's abstract. Short quotations with source; no paper is committed.

sources.cite: Wei, K., & Heim, L. (2025). Designing Incident Reporting Systems for Harms from General-Purpose AI. arXiv:2511.05914.
passages: actors submitting and receiving reports, type of incidents reported, level of risk materialization, enforcement of reporting, anonymity of reporters, and post-reporting actions
sources.use: Names post-reporting actions and near-miss reporting among the dimensions of a reporting system's design. This step measures both as they stand in force: of 81 acts after word of the two cases reached 20 doors, 6 were owed by any text; and at the maker's door before the harm, three words of the kind a near-miss scheme would collect set off none of four duties without doubt.

sources.cite: Mehta, P. (2026). Macro-Prudential AI Governance: A Two-Layer Early Warning and Response System for Frontier AI. arXiv:2607.03542.
passages: discovering a risk is not tantamount to acting on it
These are systems deployed for labs' own internal research, testing, and production workflows, as distinct from externally released products.
sources.use: Proposes early warning for internal frontier systems. The escape's model was one, an internal research prototype not meant for release: the EU's two texts reach it only through a scope they leave open (the Act excludes models used for research before they are placed on the market), and California's law turns on a compute threshold the maker says its models fall below. Inside the maker, three words came before the harm, and the public record shows none of them reaching a public body before it.

sources.cite: Sidhu, H. K., Scholefield, R., Annan, N., Hernandez, K., Hou, I. N., Alshaikhi, A., Chin, Z. S., & Gipiškis, R. (2026). Open Problems in AI Incident Governance. arXiv:2607.05163.
passages: AI systems may produce failures after deployment that pre-deployment safety assessments do not anticipate.
there is a lack of consistency within the aspects of definitions, classification, monitoring, and reporting
sources.use: Finds definitions and reporting inconsistent across frameworks, and frames incident governance after deployment. This reading takes one case before deployment through four definitions in force: the same word is coded differently by each, and every one of the six cells left in doubt before the harm turns on a term (a breach's seriousness, a model's scope, a risk's materiality) that no text assigns anyone to settle.

sources.cite: Gruetzemacher, R. (2026). AI Loss of Control Incident Management: Response & Resilience. arXiv:2605.30406.
passages: current literature focuses almost exclusively on alignment and prevention
sources.use: Sets out how a loss-of-control incident should be managed once it is known. This step asks who is obliged to begin: no public body's act in the two cases was owed by an AI instrument, and the one clock the record shows set on a public body, California's executive order of 18 September, asked for recommendations on the law two months after the harm and was met on the day.

sources.cite: Bollinger, S., Aboserie, N., Coakley, A., Lee, C.-H., & Mathlouthi, T. (2026). Signals in the Noise: Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) for AI Loss of Control Detection. arXiv:2606.20610.
passages: OSINT-based detection of loss of control is partially feasible and worth building now.
sources.use: Argues for detection independent of developers. In both cases the public learned of the event from a party other than the maker, and every public body was first seen acting after that; before the harm, the only reader placed to tell whether a law's trigger had been met was the maker itself.
